stories.body:
A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies

“H istoric” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.

The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.

Mr Xi looks like the power broker bringing Moscow and Washington together, and the gracious host, in a city which showcases China’s economic and technological progress and aspirations. The contrast between the glossy metropolis and a US currently beset by glaring tech failures hitting everything from flights to banking is especially flattering. For Mr Putin, who gloated about the “humiliation” of Europe in the run-up, this meeting is an even clearer win, making him look like a superpower peer rather than the leader of a pariah nation with a struggling economy.

Mr Trump has got a red carpet embrace, another “first” to promote – preferable to headlines dwelling on the Republicans’ midterms disaster – and the congenial company of strongmen. His nation has less to celebrate. Mr Trump seems to see meeting longstanding US allies as at best a chore. His bruising tariffs and nakedly transactional approach to security, as well as his love of autocrats, have pushed countries like the Philippines – which hosted the US president en route to China – into hedging their bets.

Mr Trump is not expected to raise Nvidia and suspected Chinese espionage – perhaps not least because his closeness to Jensen Huang, the company’s ousted CEO, makes the issue at least as discomfiting for him as it is for Beijing. The US president is unlikely to embarrass the two countries that are central to Iran’s ability to resist his disastrous and illegal war, or to press China over its facilitation of Russia’s war against Ukraine . Ukraine and Taiwan have reason to be anxious any time he speaks to Mr Putin and Mr Xi. But the US president is as likely to undermine them, whether deliberately or otherwise, in bilaterals or via a throwaway remark.

Comparisons to the 1945 Yalta summit of Joseph Stalin, Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill – which divided up Europe – grotesquely overstate the importance of a meeting scheduled to last less than an hour. Mr Xi does not do spontaneity, and is unlikely to be lured into sudden announcements. And despite the surface amity, the three still have strongly competing interests. China’s threat to rare earths brought a trade truce, but skirmishes continue. Mr Trump has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation . While China is arming itself at worrying speed, its arsenal is still dwarfed by those of the US and Russia.

Talking to rivals and adversaries is not inherently unwise. Under another US president, a closely focused and carefully prepared trilateral on, for instance, disarmament might even be fruitful. This is not that world. This will not be that meeting.

stories.title: Ted Cruz-led committee approves Trump FCC nominee 15-0 as Democrats boycott vote
stories.summary: Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues.

A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote.

All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent. “We’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs,” Cruz said at today’s hearing.

Nominees are vetted in committees first, and then seek require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January.

Although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz said Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.”

Technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. Until today.”

False testimony allegation

At a hearing last week, Thumann said she never worked with Carr on media-related topics, leading to accusations that she provided false testimony. “I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related issues,” Thumann said after Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked, “Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?”

“It appears that Ms. Thumann misled the Committee and offered false testimony, seriously calling into question her judgment and character and impeding the Committee’s work in determining whether she should be seated on the Commission,” Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz yesterday. “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media-related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount.”

The FCC website describes Thumann as senior counsel to Carr on matters before the Wireline Bureau, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, and the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau. Emails obtained in a public records request by the group Protect Democracy show she had some involvement in media-related matters.

Thumann provided follow-up responses to senators’ questions this week. She said that her work sometimes includes “reviewing documents or filings in a matter outside of my designated portfolio. However, I did not have any conversations with Paramount, CBS, or Skydance related to the merger.”

Emails touched on 60 Minutes complaints

Thumann has been referred to as Thumann Severs in the nomination process, but she uses the name Thumann.

Luján wrote that Thumann “played a role in processing informal complaints related to” alleged news distortion on CBS’s 60 Minutes , and that “she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” However, Thumann was only a recipient of the Kimmel-related emails we found in a search of the messages.

The emails do show that Thumann approved language used in a response the FCC gave to complaints about the alleged news distortion in a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. The response informed people who submitted complaints that they should instead submit comments on an FCC docket that had been set up for the 60 Minutes proceeding.

“Hi Kristi, I have confirmed with the Chairman and Erin that we would like for complainants to be encouraged to resubmit their news distortion complaints in the relevant ECFS [Electronic Comment Filing System] proceeding,” Thumann wrote. “Can you please work on some draft language to send to consumers that would advise them on this step (including how to use ECFS)?”

Democrats aimed to prevent quorum

Democrats announced yesterday that they would try to prevent a quorum for today’s vote. They objected to adding a third Republican to the committee while a Democratic seat remains empty.

“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Cantwell said in a statement.

Cantwell and other Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Cruz urging him to cancel the vote, while quoting his own words from 2014. “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the Democratic committee members said.

Cruz said today that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January. But today is November 18.” Cruz said there is “ample precedent” for advancing nominations in a lame-duck session.

Senate Commerce Committee rules state that a quorum for nomination votes requires a “majority of the members, which includes at least one minority member.” But a Cruz spokesperson pointed to certain clauses regarding committee quorums in Senate rules when contacted by Ars today.

In the Standing Rules of the Senate , paragraph 7 of rule XXVI says that “no measure or matter or recommendation shall be reported from any committee unless a majority of the committee were physically present,” and does not have any requirement for minority members to be present. Elsewhere, the Senate rules say that when a committee reports a measure to the Senate floor, “no point of order shall lie with respect to that measure” as long as the committee took its action “in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 7 of rule XXVI.”

While committees can have different quorum rules, a Cruz spokesperson said this functions as a “cleansing clause” so that “earlier procedural irregularities, such as a violation of a committee rule, cannot be used to invalidate the vote on the Senate floor.”

Cruz rejects paired nominations

FCC nominations have traditionally been paired with one Republican and one Democrat when there is an empty seat for each party. But Cruz said that’s not a requirement.

“There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs… the law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party,” Cruz said during the Republican-only meeting.

The Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority. It says, “The maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”

Republicans would have a 3-1 majority on the FCC if Thumann is confirmed by the Senate. The sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, would have to leave at the end of 2027 if Trump does not nominate her for another term.

“There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks… Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner,” Democrats told Cruz in their letter this week.

stories.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
stories.summary: China worries the scandal could ramp up pressure on the US to further restrict the sale of advanced chips.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026

Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.

For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.

Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.

US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.

The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.

For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.

Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.

Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.

Watch: Jensen Huang speaks to the BBC's Faisal Islam in 2025

Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.

The BBC has approached the White House for comment.

Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".

"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.

The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".

Another 'spy balloon' incident?

For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.

The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.

It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.

Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim , advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.

Now that opening may be under threat.

History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.

Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.

The suspected Chinese spy balloon was shot down days after it was spotted over the US

But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.

The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.

"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.

"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.

The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.

"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.

Trump-Xi summit unlikely to collapse

Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.

China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.

Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.

The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.

He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.

Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.

The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.

It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.

Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.

One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.

Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.

That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

stories.body:
In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours

In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power” .

Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister.

In Donald Trump , Putin has a ready supplier of balm to soothe his injured vanity. The US president has a shallow, venal concept of power. He is impressed by gilded palaces and heavily armed thugs. He feels thwarted by American democracy and envies tyrants who operate without equivalent restraint. Since Trump measures greatness in a country by its leader’s contempt for smaller nations and appetite for self-enriching plunder, he willingly promotes Russia back to the top tier.

That is the significance to Putin of a three-way summit with Trump and China’s Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday. It confers trappings of parity with the world’s two genuine superpowers. That is a win for Russia, regardless of whether anything of substance is agreed.

The agenda is vague. The Chinese foreign ministry has said the discussion will focus on “ safeguarding world peace ” and “promoting strategic stability in major-power relations”. Xi will be satisfied with the projection of China as convener of a new world order. Trump has said he expects the conversation to cover denuclearisation, Iran, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”.

The image of three leaders calibrating the balance of global power has been compared to Yalta, February 1945: Roosevelt, Stalin and Churchill drawing up plans for postwar Europe . That was a week-long conference where military allies were settling the fate of a defeated enemy. The analogy is revealing mostly as an expression of anxiety in those who will not be present.

For many Europeans, Yalta conjures memories of cynical partition, with eastern nations condemned to decades of Soviet captivity. The fear in Kyiv is that Putin will use his privileged access to Trump’s ear to pour in poisonous theories about the origins of the Ukraine war and how to end it – a twisted narrative of Nato provocation, irresistible Russian superiority and the need for Europe to stop wasting money and US military hardware on a losing cause.

The exclusion of European democracies from the room in Shenzhen is partly just a function of the conversation happening on the sidelines of a summit for countries with Pacific coasts. But it probes a deep strategic insecurity. Ukraine’s continental allies have asserted their rights to be part of any peace process but not found a way to turn that entitlement into a collective position, coordinated by a figure with diplomatic gravitas.

After a round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Jared Kushner, one of Trump’s envoys, made the reassuring statement that a deal could not be done “without Europeans being at the table”. By contrast, Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, accused the Europeans of lacking serious intent to find solutions. He dismissed their delegation to the Gulf as “tourists” who might as well “chat in the hotel bar”.

That is standard Kremlin trolling, but it cuts with a shard of truth. It points to an old problem, often described with the apocryphal tale of Henry Kissinger complaining that there was no number to call when he wanted to speak to Europe. The challenge is more acute today. The institutional and economic foundations of European influence are under assault. Trump is ambivalent at best about Nato. His administration is protectionist and nationalist. Maga ideology casts liberal democratic Europe as a moribund civilisation erasing itself with mass immigration.

China treats Europe as a bundle of consumers for manufactured exports whose politicians usually, by default, defer to Washington. The EU has ambitions of “strategic autonomy” but the process is slow and expensive. It means evolution from soft power – rivalling the US and China in economic heft as a single market whose regulations set global standards – to something a lot harder. European electorates may despise Trump and fear Putin, but they are not all comfortable with the choices that follow if the remedy is a shift in budget priorities to higher defence spending.

A lot of European politics in recent years has been driven with a longing eye on the rear view mirror, wondering if there is a way back to the old world of open trade, respect for international law, a White House that wouldn’t abet the Kremlin in an imperial land grab. But there is growing recognition that Europe’s future cannot resemble its recent past.

The UK is part of that story, and Andy Burnham has understood the implications. In a speech on Monday , the prime minister expanded his criticism of Brexit from the economic to the geopolitical arena. It was, he said, “the first domino to fall” in a pattern of global fragmentation. It introduced a schism in European alliances that was “exactly what our enemies wanted”. Burnham’s audit of the costs in forfeited trade was familiar enough, but he moved the argument up a gear by noting that withdrawal from the top table of European decision-making has cost Britain power and influence in the world. That is something continuity Brexiters cannot compute.

after newsletter promotion

As Burnham finds his pro-European voice, the old Eurosceptic myth-making industrial complex is grinding back into motion. Newspapers have published tenuous stories about the cost of restored alignment with Brussels and hypothetical migrant influxes. Veterans of the leave campaign are limbering up for a dismal dance around the 2016 totem pole. It is rotten from exposure to a decade of international storms.

Britain is a regional power that undervalued the amplifying effect of EU membership. The benefits of being in the club felt enough like great-power status to fool Eurosceptics into thinking they could go it alone. They cling to that delusion. Kemi Badenoch has written about Britain having “latent great power attributes”. She doesn’t have a theory of how those dormant traits will be awoken in a world carved into continental blocs.

Burnham’s plan is hardly precise, but at least he starts with facts: Britain is a European country; Europe will be safer and richer if it pools its resources; the UK should not want to be on the margin.

A summit where Xi, Putin and Trump claim to be deciding the fate of the world may not yield much in the way of concrete deals, but it still contains a warning to European democracies. And a choice. One option is to boost leverage through closer continental cooperation. The alternative is flight into fantasies of immaculate national sovereignty and resurrected historical grandeur. One of those routes is a way for Europe to grow autonomy, security and prosperity in the 21st century. The other is the path of bitter self-defeat modelled by Brexit .

stories.title: Google rejects UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
stories.summary: This comes after Brand's wife shared a message from him in which he claimed his innocence.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 18 November 2026

Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.

The Prison Service of England and Wales submitted the request. A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed.

The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

There was no immediate comment from Google when approached by BBC News.

On Sunday, his wife Laura had shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a handwritten message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

The MoJ spokesperson added that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".

The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that the video be removed on the basis that they believed it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.

The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.

The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.

The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken.

Brand's message prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against him, said she found the message shared on the couple's Sunday Service show "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.

Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme this week.

She is one of the women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell criticised media outlets earlier on Wednesday for playing extracts of the message, saying they should not have "amplified" his words.

Speaking to LBC, she described Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".

In 2023, YouTube suspended Brand's channels from making money from adverts for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy", shortly after he was accused of rape and sexual assaults between 2006 and 2013.

The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site.

Meanwhile, his social media accounts on Meta platforms - Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

stories.title: Trump abandons his FDA nominee, and Senate scraps vote on his NSF pick
stories.summary: "This time requires leadership and fortitude," Senator Bill Cassidy said.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
“This time requires leadership and fortitude,” Senator Bill Cassidy said.

In the span of less than 24 hours, two Trump administration nominees have suffered sudden blows—Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration and his pick to lead the National Science Foundation.

Late Tuesday evening, Axios reported that the White House had abruptly withdrawn its controversial nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA. Overton, a top conservative domestic policy aide in the White House, has drawn criticism and skepticism from Republicans and Democrats alike over her stances on vaccines, abortion, vapes, and birth control. Overton opposes abortion—though perhaps not strongly enough for some Republicans—and supported Trump and Kennedy’s decried anti-vaccine policies and statements, vexing Democrats.

In her confirmation hearing in September, Overton consistently stonewalled senators on every topic, refusing to directly answer even softball questions from friendly Republicans, leaving lawmakers on both sides of the aisle openly frustrated. The questions she dodged included those on how she would handle the FDA’s current safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, which extensive data has established is extremely safe. She also wouldn’t say whether she agreed with Trump when he falsely claimed the measles vaccine is “quite lethal” or that children are given vaccine doses the “size of a soda bottle.” Overton repeatedly refused to answer whether Trump could ever be wrong.

Axios quoted a senior Trump administration official as saying that Overton’s nomination was dropped because she “lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation.”

The Senate’s Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee, chaired by Bill Cassidy (R-La.), was scheduled to vote on Overton’s nomination Wednesday. In a social media post Tuesday night, after her nomination was withdrawn, Cassidy said he believed she had a “viable confirmation path.” But he said the nomination was “abandoned” after some anti-abortion senators sought commitments from her that they couldn’t get. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments,” Cassidy said.

“Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats,” Cassidy noted.

O’Neill canceled

After Overton’s last-minute withdrawal, the HELP committee’s agenda for Wednesday was updated again this morning to scrap a scheduled vote on Jim O’Neill, who was Trump’s nominee to run the NSF.

O’Neill has been criticized for lacking the science experience needed to run the foundation. In the past, O’Neill worked as a Silicon Valley investor and entrepreneur and became a close ally of Peter Thiel. But under Trump, O’Neill has been the deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services and served as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. O’Neill took over the latter role after the former director, Susan Monarez, was ousted from it less than a month after her Senate confirmation. She later told Senators Kennedy fired her for refusing to blindly approve vaccine recommendations from his anti-vaccine advisors.

In remarks this morning , Cassidy said that O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from [Health] Secretary [Robert F.] Kennedy [Jr.].” As an example, Cassidy specifically referenced O’Neill’s role in the firing of Monarez. “Several members of the [HELP] committee had concerns regarding this,” Cassidy said.

“This time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy added.

The NSF has been hard hit by the Trump administration and actions by Elon Musk’s DOGE. The NSF has been forced to cancel hundreds of research grants and taken brutal cuts to its budget and staff in the past two years. In April, the Trump administration also terminated all members of the board that steers the NSF, called the National Science Board. Former members feared that it would make way for O’Neill to stack the board with political allies, pointing to how Trump filled the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology with tech billionaires —including leaders of Meta, Google, Oracle, and Nvidia—instead of top scientists and researchers.

stories.body:
Outages happen, but we deserve a resilient internet where no one outage at one company can put people at risk and disrupt the global economy. We can only get there by addressing an over-reliance on a few cloud monopolists through effective antitrust laws and interoperability requirements.

Service outages, like we’ve seen recently at Microsoft , Apple *, banks , courts , airlines , and elsewhere, can be more than an annoying hurdle. Losing a vital service due to an error can cause the same impacts as a government-ordered internet shutdown—people losing access to vital information and lines of communication. As usual, the greatest harms are faced by people on the margins globally.

There’s not much hope in companies out-nerding these issues either. Technical errors will always exist, whether it’s a bug , negligence from an administrator, or a malicious attack. The problem is an over-reliance on any one company or system when these inevitable outages occur. It’s a matter of public safety and economic stability that policymakers mitigate the impact of these disruptions before they occur.

In order to do so, we must ensure antitrust prevents providers of key technical systems from becoming too big to fail.

The harms inflicted by tech monopolies go beyond monetary costs to the end user. In fact, monopolists can often offer lower prices, or even offer free services, thanks to their greater scale and incentive to shut out competitors using free-flowing investment capital . The problem is this puts a few tech companies in a position of incredible influence. The true cost is a loss of control when our private data, access to knowledge, and free expression all become mediated by tools owned by a handful of billionaires.

Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone.

This isn’t just a bad deal for us as individuals. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. When everything from daily tasks to national security is reliant on a few digital monocultures , one mistake or exploit can cascade into an explosive impact. The risks multiply in the current investment climate, where financial markets reward companies that strip-mine redundancy and resiliency from critical systems. Even if you see the problem coming, an outage that hits clients, suppliers, collaborators or loved ones proves just as disruptive. We need to remove these chokepoints for good, which means a digital sovereignty movement that makes the web more free by design—not just importing existing levers of control into another nation's borders.

Central to this effort must be undercutting platform control by fostering interoperability , i.e. when tools are made to be compatible among competitors. When this is done carefully , it’s not only easier to switch to better alternatives, we wind up with more alternatives as it becomes more viable to compete or offer complementary tools alongside existing systems.

This is what made systems like email great. You could choose your own apps and services, even using several simultaneously, and never lose touch with a contact. Early architects of the internet did not take reliable hosting for granted. Services were often on a machine a few rooms over, and needed to be prepared for the occasional interruption of service.

But in the age of hyperscalers and massive data centers, the infrastructure underlying the web isn’t owned by many scattered IT departments, it’s rented from a handful of “cloud” providers. These providers managed to scale up quickly and replace interoperability with walled gardens, enticing customers with lower costs while making it costly to leave and tightly controlling how services behave . Once in control, these platforms have every incentive to enshittify their services and devalue their workers , delivering an increasingly shoddy and restrictive service.

This context makes building interoperability an act of defiance—often coming from the sweat of open source developers. These projects may be tolerated by monopolists in the short term, but can be one boardroom decision away from being broken entirely. A better internet means championing these creators through funding, liability protections, and requiring big players to cooperate. Here is what lawmakers should do:

Federal and state legislators should—

Defend competitive compatibility. Developers merely providing alternative interfaces for tools should be shielded from liability. In the U.S., that means explicit protections under DMCA , CFAA , and corporate Terms of Service agreements. These protections should cover shared protocols and APIs as well as automated content retrieval through scraping .

Encourage interoperability. Lawmakers should force open key aspects of platform infrastructure by requiring big tech to support: (1) data portability, so users can move to a new service (2) back-end interoperability, to support more tools with competitive compatibility and (3) delegability, so people are not prevented from having code act on their behalf. So far, the Digital Markets Act in the EU has provided some positive examples of such legislation

Fund open source. In order to be sustainable, interoperable tools and standards cannot rely solely on corporate interest and volunteer labor. Programs like the EU Sovereign Tech Fund could help create viable alternatives within and beyond the borders of the EU.

Municipalities and institutions should—

Buy interoperable services. At any level, government agencies should set minimum interoperability requirements in procurement and hold a competitive bidding process to evaluate vendors’ privacy, security and lock-in risks. Agencies dependent on a sole provider, including through cooperative purchase agreements, are stuck with corporate price-gouging and even higher switching costs.

Fund Departments of Information Technology. Cloud services are often adopted to offset spending on IT professionals but, when these departments atrophy, institutions become even more reliant on the cloud providers. Maintaining in-house talent prevents this cycle of dependency and improves emergency responses to outages.

Adopt a plus-one approach to public communications. Institutions shouldn’t force citizens into walled gardens just to access public communications. In addition to posts to corporate social media, government agencies should share the same information on an open protocol— whether it’s bluesky, the fediverse, or just an RSS feed . By putting these in the open, more people will have access to urgent alerts and can create new useful tools.

Building a more resilient and democratic internet is possible, and many people are already hard at work doing just that. Above are some necessary steps to get corporate and government interests out of the way of rewilding the net with greater community and individual controls. The dream of the internet as a digital commons operating for the public good is not dead yet, and is worth fighting for.

stories.title: Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts
stories.summary: In her decision, Judge Emma Kelly says there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.

stories.body:
The injunction granted by the High Court prevents Ryan Bridge and Raise the Colours from attaching flags and other items to public property

Published 18 November 2026

Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure across the city.

The authority sought the order after thousands of St George's flags and union jacks were put up by supporters of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from summer 2025 onwards.

Council lawyers argued the displays created safety risks and fuelled tensions, while campaigners said the move would restrict freedom of expression.

Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.

In her ruling, the judge said it would last until trial or further order of the court.

The order applies to Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.

It also grants a power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning police could arrest someone without a warrant if they are suspected of breaching the injunction.

The council said anyone who breaches the order could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.

The local authority sought the injunction after thousands of St George's flags and union flags were attached to lamp-posts and bridges in Birmingham from summer 2025 onwards.

Lawyers acting for the council argued the displays could pose safety risks, obstruct visibility and contribute to tensions and disorder. The application also referred to reported incidents of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction connected to flags being put up in the city.

The court heard that, on one occasion, a man suffered a broken leg when he was struck by a cherry picker being used while flags were being installed.

The case followed similar legal action in Oxfordshire, where the county council secured a permanent injunction against four named individuals over flags attached to lamp-posts and other highway structures.

Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge had argued an injunction would breach the European Convention on Human Rights

Bridge opposed the injunction, arguing it would interfere with rights to freedom of expression and protest under the European Convention on Human Rights.

His barrister, Liam Wells, told the court the campaign amounted to political expression protected by the convention and argued the injunction would have a "chilling effect" on those rights.

In her ruling, Kelly stressed the order was not a ban on displaying flags.

"The interim injunction needs to be understood for what it is," she said.

"It is not the court nor the claimant 'banning the union jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like.

"Whilst the interim injunction order will cover flags of all types, it is limited in scope to the restraint of unauthorised flags attached to highway street furniture or infrastructure, and to the restraint of associated conduct, within the administrative area of Birmingham."

She added that concerns the injunction would unduly restrict free expression were "unwarranted" and said she was satisfied it was "just and convenient" to grant the order.

The council said anyone who breaches the injunction could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court

The injunction covers all unauthorised flags attached to street furniture, regardless of the type of flag involved.

Birmingham City Council's cabinet member for equalities, communities and social justice, Jane Baston, welcomed the ruling and described it as an "important step" in tackling unauthorised attachments to public highways.

She said residents remained free to display flags on their own property and said the council's approach had been "proportionate and evidence-led".

Councillor Jane Baston called the interim injunction an "important step" for the authority

Councillor Robert Alden, leader of Birmingham local Conservatives, criticised the authority's decision to pursue the injunction, saying it should focus on resolving the city's bin strike and improving basic services.

Campaign group Brummies United Against Racism & Hate Crime welcomed the ruling, describing it as "a welcome decision and long overdue".

A further hearing is due to take place in Birmingham on Thursday.

stories.title: Surveillance Isn't Safety: A Comic About Organizing Against Flock and Other Foes
stories.summary: In the new comic "Surveillance Isn't Safety"—available for free today— cartoonist Bryn Adams explores the growing movement against mass surveillance through their involvement in the community fight against Flock Safety in Cleveland, Ohio. It's a personal journey that will resonate widely with residents in hundreds of cities where communities are drawing the line against automated license plate readers (ALPRs). Jump to the Comic Or download the PDF Published in collaboration between EFF and Crucial Comix , Bryn's comic captures the authenticity of the grassroot backlash against the surveillance industry—undercutting Flock founder Garrett Langley's latest dubious defense that public opposition of his company's product isn't real. At the International Association of Chiefs of Police conference this fall, Langley accused the anti-surveillance activism of being driven by Russian bots and as being "inorganic." He pointed to the fact that many local groups were using similar language in their protest signs as supposed proof, when in reality, shared slogans are one of the hallmarks of a social movement. This was all misdirection from the grim realities that Flock and other ALPR systems facilitate: the mistakes are real; the abuse is real; the racism is real; and the targeting of dissenters , migrants , and abortion seekers is real. And, importantly, the cancelled contracts are real. Bryn's comic sheds light on the real abuses and threats driving communities to mobilize against Flock, Axon, and other ALPR vendors. It shows that coast-to-coast activism doesn't happen overnight—any more than a comic appears out of thin air as a finished product. As advisors on the cartoon, EFF watched how Bryn's script evolved from rough sketches to penciled drawings, then to inked and shaded panels, mirroring how the long-running movement against mass surveillance has steadily snowballed over the last few years. There is nothing “inorganic” about either: Both are built on passion, commitment, and putting in the work. Increase in October piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy

Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January

Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October after petrol prices increased and diesel hit a record high amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose from 3.5% in September and was in line with City economists’ forecasts.

As households brace for the colder winter months with household gas and electricity costs soaring, the latest figures push the headline inflation rate to the highest level in a year.

In a reading underscoring the pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates, the ONS said fuel prices were the major contributor. Annual costs of raw materials and goods leaving factories also continued to climb, driven by rising energy and crude oil prices amid the Iran war.

Fuel prices for motorists rose at an annual rate of 33.2%, the largest increase since July 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sparked a global surge in energy prices.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p a litre between September and October to reach 174.7p a litre, the highest level in four years. Diesel prices rose by 7p a litre to 199.5p a litre, the highest price on records dating back to 1996.

Andy Burnham’s government has pledged to offer support for households grappling with a fresh cost of living squeeze as the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up inflation worldwide.

At the budget last month the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans for a £100 winter handout for 20m households to cushion the blow from the global economic storm.

The latest inflation figures took into account a 4% increase in the Ofgem energy price cap from the start of October.

A forecast from the consultancy Cornwall Insight on Wednesday predicted a 26% jump in energy bills in Great Britain from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household.

Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Earlier this month, Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% and warned further increases in the cost of borrowing might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said the longer the conflict continued the more likely it was that rate increases would be needed, despite a recent drop in global energy prices since the US midterm elections.

Speaking at a conference in London on Tuesday, Bailey said inflation was “probably going to be a bit less” than the 5% forecast made by the Bank earlier this month.

after newsletter promotion

However, he said that if the war pushed energy prices higher, the “more likely persistent inflationary effects will take hold and the higher the level of interest rates will need to be”.

Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point increases before the end of next year. Analysts said the Bank could raise borrowing costs from as early as next month.

Core inflation – which excludes volatile energy, food, alcohol and tobacco prices – was unchanged at 2.8%, matching economists’ forecasts. Services inflation, which the Bank has been monitoring closely for evidence of domestic inflationary pressures becoming entrenched, also held steady at 3.7%, slightly below City predictions for a rate of 3.8%.

Air fares rose by 1.8% between September and October amid an increase in long-haul ticket prices – offset by a downward effect from European flights. Prices for alcohol and tobacco also rose, by 4.5%, influenced by the timing of an increase in tobacco duty at the start of the month.

Food prices rose at the slowest rate since September 2021, at 0.9%, down from 1.3% in September.

Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said: “The conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world.

“The household energy payment, announced in our budget, is providing £100 directly into 20 million bank accounts in January, which will help to give families breathing space now.

“The budget also started the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good, including an end to levies on household bills, scrapping standing charges and ensuring Britain is better protected from global shocks in the future.”

Closing post

Time to wrap up

Jensen Huang has thrown his hat into the ring to return to his role running Nvidia, less than a week after being ousted amid an alleged spy scandal.

Huang has issued a statement admitting making “serious mistakes” in his personal life – a nod to his previous admission of cheating on his wife, allegedly with a suspected Chinese spy.

He says:

double quotation mark I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.

But Huang also indicated he would be happy to return to his role, saying:

double quotation mark Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Here’s the full story:

Huang , and Nvidia’s top lawyer, have agreed to testify to Congressional committees next month .

Stock markets have fallen across Europe and in New York, ahead of Nvidia’s results after today’s closing Wall Street bell.

The tech-focused Nasdaq led the fallers, down 1.6%.

In London, the FTSE 100 posted its biggest one-day fall since March, falling by 1.76%.

Investors are eager to hear tonight whether Nvidia is sticking to its financial guidance, following the scandal which forced out CEO Jensen Huang last week.

The company has already announced the creation of a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee , to keep tabs on its operations.

Two US departments have confirmed that Megaspeed is being investigated for violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia’s chips to China.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.

China has hit back after the US closed a loophole which allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia-powered data centres in third-party countries.

China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing would take “necessary measures” to safeguard its own interests, saying:

double quotation mark “The US has repeatedly overstretched the concept of national security, abused export controls and even interfered in China’s normal trade and technological cooperation with other countries, unjustifiably suppressing the development of China’s high-tech industries.”

Why Huang should not be reinstated

Jensen Huang should not be reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO, argues Jeffrey Sonnenfeld , the Lester Crown Professor of Leadership Practice at the Yale School of Management .

Writing in Time Magazine today , Sonnenfeld argues that Nvidia’s board were wise to closed the door on Huang’s return, and shouldn’t let it be forced open again.

Sonnenfeld writes:

double quotation mark That door should stay shut. Over 33 years, Huang built the company at the center of the AI era, but in our view, his conduct nevertheless made his position untenable. He misled directors about undisclosed relationships and oversaw a firm no one could check—a breakdown in trust that was magnified in China, where he advocated loosening export controls even as restricted chips reached Chinese military units and a Shanghai facility tied to Alice Huang’s network. The political push to restore him rests on the billions his most prominent advocates have riding on his customer-financing web and on misleading geopolitical spin, at the expense of genuine shareholder concerns and national defense.

Sonnenfeld also argues that a board that can be overruled by a petition has “no function”, concluding:

double quotation mark Nvidia’s directors deferred to Huang for years and intervened late, and reversing course under outside pressure now would merely extend a habit of deference. Instead, the board should let its investigation finish, restore standalone Singapore revenue disclosures, and select a successor on the merits. Huang spent 33 years building an enterprise the AI era cannot do without. Now comes the defining test of a great company—whether it can outlast the person who built it.

FTSE 100 posts biggest drop since March

London’s stock market has just recorded its biggest one-day drop since the first month of the Iran war.

The FTSE 100 share index has closed down 191.68 points, or -1.76%, at 10,689 points.

That’s its biggest percentage drop since 19 March this year.

Jensen Huang: I love our country, and I love Nvidia

Here’s the full statement issued by Jensen Huang , signalling he would like to return to his former job running Nvidia .

double quotation mark Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

This is quite the intervention from Jensen Huang , just five hours before Nvidia is due to release its latest financial results.

It makes it harder for the company’s board to avoid questions about its succession plans, and heaps the pressuer on interim CEO Colette Kress to calm investors’ nerves about the company’s outlook.

Jensen Huang says he is prepared to return as Nvidia CEO

Newsflash: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has issued a statement saying he would be “honoured” to return to the role, less than a week after resigning.

In a statement issued to the media, Huang – whe quit last week over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy – says:

double quotation mark “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret.

Last weekend, an open letter called on Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang while an independent investigation was conducted.

Today, Huang says:

double quotation mark “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

However, Nvidia’s board indicated yesterday they are not considering reinstating Huang as CEO….

Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer at International Services, says Nvidia is confronting several crises at once:

An employee rebellion: Growing internal pressure to bring Huang back, with warnings that critical AI talent could walk away.

A leadership vacuum: Can Kress reassure investors, customers and employees while the board searches for a permanent CEO?

A Wall Street confidence test: Will strong earnings be enough to stabilize the stock, or has the leadership crisis fundamentally changed Nvidia’s valuation?

Washington and China: New scrutiny of Nvidia’s China-related business and national security questions adds another layer of uncertainty.

The future of AI: Could a prolonged crisis at the world’s leading AI chipmaker disrupt investment, innovation and the companies dependent on Nvidia’s technology?

Nearly every stock on the FTSE 100 share index is in the red today – pulling the Footsie down by 176 points, or 1.6%, to 10,707 points in late trading.

Nasdaq hits eight-month low

The US technology stock index, the Nasdaq Composite, has just hit an eight-month low, down around 1.6%.

Markets fall ahead of Nvidia's results

Stock markets on both sides of the Atlantic are dropping deeper into the red.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average is now down 1%, having lost 511 points to around 51,096 points.

And in London, the FTSE 100 index is down 1.4%, having dropped by 154 points to 10,726 points.

Investors may be getting jittery ahead of Nvidia’s results tonight, to be followed by Anthropic’s IPO on Thursday.

Reminder: Wall Street will hear from Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress , tonight, following the resignation of Jensen Huang last week after allegations that he conducted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Nvidia will also face questions about claims that billions of dollars of its chips were sold to China, and about the implications of the US closing a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia -powered data centres in other countries.

Joe Mazzola , head trading & derivatives strategist at Charles Schwab, says:

double quotation mark The chip giant typically releases results about half an hour after the close. Nvidia’s call follows at 5 p.m. ET, led by CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress. If a board member or executive besides Kress speaks prominently, speculation might rise about where they stand in the Huang succession stakes. Investors could hear plenty of scuttlebutt on the CEO topic after the call. The biggest question is whether Nvidia can keep growing parabolically without Huang at the helm. Outlook is paramount, and a devastating outcome would be if Nvidia pulls guidance. Back in August, Nvidia forecast fiscal 2028 revenue growth of 70%. See if the company sticks to that. Export controls on advanced chips are another topic, especially after the U.S. took new measures to limit remote access to advanced AI chips. Shares fell more than 4% Monday as investors prepared for worst-case scenarios, and big share moves are priced in for Nvidia depending on the outcome. If the call gets an optimistic take, the entire sector could feel relief. Though quarterly results might seem secondary, earnings are seen up 90.4% to $2.48 per share and revenue is seen up 91.3% to $109.1 billion.

stories.body:
It’s that time of year when Christmas adverts start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

Yet companies are increasingly using artificial intelligence ( AI ) to produce their ads. Last year proved how quickly that strategy can backfire. In the Netherlands, McDonald’s pulled an AI-generated Christmas ad depicting chaotic holiday mishaps after just three days following fierce backlash over the undisclosed usage.

This kind of omission is now restricted under new EU transparency rules that govern how AI-generated content is labelled. Coca-Cola’s 2025 festive campaign drew similar criticism. The advert featured AI-generated scenery and animals that many viewers found uncanny .

Undeterred, this year brands including Very and Plusnet have pressed ahead with AI productions. Because UK law does not require on-screen disclosure, their use of the technology is often tucked away in separate press releases and trade announcements rather than flagged to viewers. Even so, the UK Advertising Standards Authority prohibits misleading omissions if an advert falsely implies human creation to deceive consumers.

Read more: What does an ‘AI-generated’ label in advertising actually tell us?

Other brands are more subtle with their AI use. While Royal Mail’s 2025 Christmas ad relied on traditional live-action footage, it recently emerged that the campaign used an AI voiceover to narrate the spot.

Replacing human performers – even behind the microphone – has fuelled growing anxiety among both industry insiders and the general public, echoing the fears that sparked the 2023 Hollywood writers’ and actors’ strikes .

Losing trust in animated ads

This growing scepticism means even traditional animation is no longer safe from scrutiny. Dior’s Christmas short film , for example, has generated suspicions among some viewers. Described as hand-drawn and directed by French animator Sylvain Chomet, with an all-star cast featuring Rihanna and Robert Pattinson, it centres on the fashion designer Christian Dior’s friendship with film star Marlene Dietrich.

Commenters praised its authentic visual appearance, while a behind the scenes page was published on Dior’s website highlighting the actors and design sketches, warding off accusations of AI-generation.

Despite this, some viewers believed that Dior’s advert showed several hallmarks of AI. A telltale sign of AI-generated content is garbled hands and fingers. Some viewers pointed to what they perceived as missing fingers and strange hand transitions in the advert.

In an interview with Variety, Chomet and producer Aton Soumache insisted that the advert was hand-drawn and generative AI was never used. But they have confirmed using a process known as “automated interpolation” to generate intermediate frames as “a very small part of the process” for the “repetitive, mechanical part of animation, not the creative work”. Automated interpolation is a standard digital animation tool that precedes AI, but now often involves its use.

The Dior case is illustrative of how vigilant audiences have become about AI use. Just as the presence of deepfakes risks undermining our trust in all images online, a few undisclosed AI-produced adverts can lead to scepticism of all advertising as viewers hunt for evidence of brands cutting corners rather than hiring creatives.

Why care about AI in ads?

Even when specific accusations prove unfounded, the broader shift in advertising toward undisclosed generative AI raises deeper ethical and aesthetic questions for the industry as a whole.

AI models are often trained on artists’ work without compensation and threaten to put them out of work – not to mention AI datacentres’ impact on communities and the environment .

There’s also an irony in major brands baulking at the tedious task of getting the details right, and giving a misleading impression of fully human creation. These moral defects can diminish our aesthetic experience of AI adverts.

But putting aside morality, the revelation of AI use renders ads aesthetically worse in another way. Philosophers of art argue that forgeries are worse as artworks because they misrepresent achievement. We usually appreciate what the artist did in creating a work. So when we learn that a painting is not a genuine Vermeer, but a 20th century forgery by Van Meegeren, we judge it differently. (One philosopher even likens this betrayal to sexual infidelity – perhaps a bit much!)

Similarly, when we discover a beautiful, animated Christmas ad was produced with AI, we might lose appreciation for its creative process. The appearance of delicately hand-animated characters is a façade, generated not by artistic imagination but raw computational power. It’s not fraud, but it diminishes the experience.

Using AI to assist in creating complex scenery isn’t easy, and there can be skill to its use – some philosophers liken it to gardening . But it’s not the real process of hand-drawing and animation. To present it as such is a misrepresentation of achievement, imitating a style without the requisite labour behind it.

In response to these quandaries, some brands have taken to detailing the human processes behind their animated Christmas ads. Prada’s campaign emphasises traditional hand-drawn animation, with a separate behind-the-scenes video highlighting its artists. Others have followed suit. Barbour and Thatchers Cider each employed Aardman (producers of Wallace & Gromit) to hand-animate their adverts, while Etsy’s festive campaign is not-so-subtly titled “celebrate being human” . There are also video game studios which have detailed their refusal to use generative AI.

The praise showered on these traditional productions proves that audiences still care deeply about craft. A season built on warmth and sincerity cannot be manufactured by an algorithm that has never felt either.

stories.body:
Britain’s potato harvest this winter could be one of the smallest in decades.

This is partly down to the hot summer and a poor growing year. Potatoes have shallow roots and need steady moisture , so dry spells cut yield and size. Where farmers had stored water to regularly irrigate, crops fared better.

With 75% of England in drought in September, and Wales also affected by dry conditions, one model estimated that British potato yields would be 11% below average. It used the 2018 harvest as a guide . Some farmers reported a greater than 50% drop in how many potatoes they were harvesting.

Wholesale prices had already risen by more than 40% by early August . By September, big British buyers were reportedly paying more than £300 a tonne for potatoes.

The Food and Drink Federation has warned of the worst potato harvest since the 1950s .

Growers have warned supermarkets to expect smaller potatoes and tighter supplies this year, so shoppers may need to accept wider variation in size and quality . This is partly because other European countries , which often provide supplies to the UK, suffered the same hot summer, and this affected their crops, too.

But shoppers may not feel the full effect of higher wholesale prices this winter. Potatoes are more likely to become significantly more expensive next year. It is also worth noting that many supermarkets subsidise potato prices.

Lidl has announced that a 2kg bag will cost 9p in the week before Christmas. The supermarket says it is funding the low price itself, so this price tells shoppers nothing about what the crop costs to grow.

Supermarkets agree prices and volumes with farmers well in advance . Retailers may absorb some of the higher costs this year rather than risk losing customers to competitors.

The bigger question is whether British farmers will carry on planting Britain’s favourite vegetable in future, and what happens if more decide it is no longer worth the risk.

In 2025, the issue was too many potatoes heading for shops – the UK produced 5.5 million tonnes , 8.5% more than the year before. This caused prices paid to farmers to collapse.

By February 2026, top-quality maris piper potatoes were fetching about £180 a tonne on the open market, less than half the £400 of a year earlier. Contract prices for the following year were also weaker .

Growers did what economics predicts: they planted less. Analysts put this year’s area in Great Britain at around 101,000 hectares , well below the 117,500 recorded in 2020 .

Then came the heat and drought.

Why can’t farmers cash in?

Higher prices should encourage farmers to plant more. But a price spike helps only those with potatoes to sell at open-market rates. Most crops are grown under contract, and growers who struggle to deliver the agreed tonnage or quality may miss out .

Some big buyers that normally rely on contracts are buying open-market potatoes as fast as they can, so growers with uncommitted crops may do well .

Meanwhile, costs for farmers keep climbing. Conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy and fertiliser costs . Labour and machinery are also more expensive.

Meanwhile, the end of the basic payment scheme (an annual payment for farmers that followed environmental guidelines) and controversies about its replacements may have removed a financial cushion that once helped farms through bad years.

The potato contract price is fixed in advance, so growers have little room to pass costs on. Tighter margins are also hitting buyers, packers and processors, but it is growers that carry the bulk of the weather risk.

Economists call this pattern the cobweb cycle . In the textbook version, farmers plant according to last season’s price, so a glut leads to a price crash, then cuts in planting, then shortage and high prices, then over-planting again. Potatoes have followed this familiar cycle almost to the letter this year.

Yet several forces pull the other way. Speaking before the summer’s hot weather and drought, in May, Scott Walker, chief executive of the industry body representing the potato sector, GB Potatoes, said that many growers were weighing up how much exposure they would carry into 2027 . The body has warned that growers could leave the business or reduce their crop.

Contract prices were weaker this year, costs are higher, and drought has shown how exposed the crop is. Depressed cereal markets offer little alternative income, so a wholesale exit is not certain either.

Farmers will be looking closely at what supermarkets offer them in 2027. High open market prices alone will not bring growers back.

Two things matter most: the contracts offered this winter, and whether farmers can secure water supplies for next summer. Signs are that water access may remain tight. For instance, the Environment Agency put England’s reservoirs at only 54% of capacity in early October . Higher prices could prompt a rebound in planting, but a normal-weather harvest could tip the market back into glut, forcing prices down again.

Will British farmers stop planting potatoes?

In September 2026, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs saw no indication that winter supplies were at risk but added that it was too early to assess the drought’s full impact on potato production and that there was, at that point, no indication that winter potato supplies were at risk. Registered potato farmer numbers fell from about 2,466 in 2000 to 1,611 in 2020 , when the statutory body collating data on potato farmers was discontinued. But each bad year pushes more to ask whether the crop is worth it.

Tim Rooke, National Farmers’ Union potato policy group chair, said in 2025 that the UK imports approximately 1 million tonnes of frozen chips a year, because the risk against return on investment of growing potatoes is astronomically high.

A food system that leaves a shrinking number of growers to absorb the weather and price risk should not be surprised when they plant less. One option could be fairer contracts that share risk, and investment in water storage. But less certain supply chains and more volatile prices could cost shoppers more.

Climate change means water shortages and high temperatures will happen more often across Europe. Potato farmers are, therefore, likely to face these challenges more regularly in the future.

stories.summary: The post Chicago’s City Council Orders Independent Review of Finances as Scrutiny Intensifies appeared first on ProPublica .
