stories.imageAlt: A man in a suit stands at a desk in front of a microphone in a government building.
stories.body:
Skepticism from council members and the stunning resignation of the city’s chief financial officer add to tension at City Hall as the mayor seeks solutions while facing a mountain of debt.

Co-published with WTTW News

The debate over Chicago’s financial struggles — out in the open as never before — took a new turn on Wednesday as the City Council added to the scrutiny.

The City Council voted 45-5 in a special meeting to give a leading alderperson the authority to hire an outside firm to independently review Chicago’s finances.

It’s unclear if an audit would be complete in time for the City Council to consider its findings before the Dec. 29 deadline mandated by state law to pass a 2027 budget, in what likely will be contentious negotiations with Mayor Brandon Johnson. Later in the day came another sign of distress: S&P Global put the city on credit watch with a warning that the budget wrangling is likely to result in a credit downgrade within 90 days.

The intense council debate over the city’s financial future comes in the wake of a package of stories published Monday by WTTW News and ProPublica that examined how a $55 billion debt burden, decades in the making, was hampering efforts to service Chicagoans and how the Johnson administration was turning to more borrowing to plug holes, such as large police settlements.

Alderperson Pat Dowell had called for the outside review after former Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch abruptly resigned Friday over what she described as a political environment that forced her to downplay certain facts about the city’s financial situation. Gabrysch argued that her integrity would be compromised if she stayed on.

Just as Gabrysch had once been a trusted part of Johnson’s team, Dowell was once thought to be a mayoral ally. Johnson tapped Dowell, who endorsed him during the 2023 mayoral election, to lead the City Council’s Finance Committee soon after he took office.

But since then Dowell has proven to be a thorn in the mayor’s side, refusing last year to support his proposal to impose a $25 per month per employee tax on most firms that have more than 125 employees and hike the city’s personal property lease tax. (Johnson continues to push for that idea.)

The ordinance gives Dowell the authority to spend whatever is necessary “to determine whether any material or intentional misstatements of the city’s financial condition to investors, the City Council and the public have been made in any public document, presentation, offering or financial reporting within the prior three years.”

The firm, or firms, hired to conduct the review will have access to all city documents and records, and all city officials must cooperate with the probe, according to the ordinance.

“We must ensure that our math is correct,” Dowell said, vowing to act quickly. “The discrepancies over the past few weeks have been particularly disturbing to me. As my mother used to say, where there’s smoke, there’s fire.”

Johnson said he welcomed the review and will not veto the ordinance.

Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said he wasn’t certain an audit was warranted while acknowledging its importance in another way. He noted that the audit vote coupled with the inability of the council and the mayor to agree on a budget plan already may have done damage with credit rating agencies.

“The way cities make their budgets matter,” Marlowe said. “It matters that for the third year in a row that there are disagreements over basic facts.”

In short, Marlowe said, “Investors don’t like uncertainty, and this is creating a lot of uncertainty.”

Alderperson Matt Martin said Wednesday that the analysis by ProPublica and WTTW was “sobering.” He is questioning some of Johnson’s borrowing strategies.

Over the years, Chicago alderpersons have generally acquiesced to mayoral directives on finances. But that has changed under Johnson, in part due to his preference for a head tax but also because of the growing realization that the city’s finances have been undermined by a series of decisions from previous mayors .

Similarly, top administration officials generally choose to leave City Hall either quietly or with words of praise for the current mayor. That’s not how Gabrysch handled her exit.

The statement she released Friday made it clear she had severe doubts about the way Johnson was portraying the city’s debt problem. And she reiterated those concerns in a commentary in the Chicago Tribune over the weekend that also laid out her suggestions for how the city can more responsibly handle its budgeting (for example, “Don’t borrow to pay everyday bills, even if we’ve done so in the past”).

Then, in a brief interview with the Chicago Sun-Times on Monday, she said she supported calls for a financial audit.

“If this makes it easier for residents to see that Chicago actually is in a fairly dire fiscal situation where hard decisions … and shared sacrifices have to be made, that can be helpful,” Gabrysch said. “Shining some light on the city’s finances — whether or not they discover wrongdoing, but rather showing the nuances of how dire some things have become — could be worthwhile.”

Chicago’s credit rating has been plummeting, adding to the cost of borrowing and leaving the city just two or three levels above junk status among leading Wall Street rating agencies. Gabrysch had been hired just three months ago from Fitch Ratings, with an eye toward shoring up the city’s reputation.

S&P Global, one of a handful of major ratings agencies, released a statement on Wednesday about its “CreditWatch” for Chicago. It cited the intense battle over the budget and an increased likelihood that “the city will resort to significant one-time measures to balance the fiscal 2027 budget.”

That means analysts see at least a 1-in-2 chance of issuing a rating cut in the next three months.

Johnson’s administration has sought to portray Gabrysch as someone who fell short in her duties and mismanaged a major transfer of funds — characterizations she has disputed.

Read More

The mayor has dismissed the conflict that led to Gabrysch’s resignation as a “technical dispute.” When he unveiled his 2027 budget, Johnson and administration officials said 76% of the budget gap would be closed with “structural fixes” — long-term or permanent solutions — that would bring expenses in line with revenues. That could help the city avoid another credit downgrade.

But Gabrysch told the City Council on Oct. 26 that the decision to borrow $481 million to cover the cost of resolving police misconduct lawsuits in 2027 and 2028 changed that calculation, reducing the amount the gap closed with revenue the city can count on in future years to just 56%.

As recently as September, Johnson told reporters the city would not borrow to cover those costs.

If the City Council approves Johnson’s proposal to borrow $481 million, the city’s massive debt burden — which now tops $55 billion — is set to grow for the second straight year to cover the cost of running the city, a sign of financial trouble.

That distress, Johnson has argued, is largely due to the decisions of previous administrations. “It’s no secret: Our city finds itself in a precarious financial situation due to decades of mismanagement,” he said Tuesday.

stories.body:
The Justice Department has lost thousands of years of experience in Trump’s second term. Amid the brain drain, the DOJ has loosened standards to hire young attorneys as it focuses more on immigration and less on fraud and drug cases in key districts.

In early October, a recent law school graduate shared a post on LinkedIn that would have been unheard of before the second Trump administration.

After passing the bar exam, 29-year-old Preston Bigley wrote, “With this milestone complete, I will begin serving as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Criminal Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas.”

It was a remarkable achievement, considering Bigley had graduated from Texas A&M’s law school in May and had been hired by the Justice Department in August to be, as his resume notes, an “incoming” assistant U.S. attorney. That unusual title was followed by an unusual caveat: “pending bar admission.” Once officially licensed to practice the law, he updated his profile to show he had become a bona fide federal criminal prosecutor.

Bigley is one of a growing cohort of inexperienced attorneys, many of them fresh out of law school, who are being fast-tracked to fill the shoes of seasoned career prosecutors who fled or were purged from the DOJ in President Donald Trump’s second term. That brain drain, amounting to thousands of years of experience, comes as prosecutions of fraud and drugs have fallen in key districts to make way for Trump’s immigration agenda, ProPublica found.

Across the country, ProPublica identified more than 50 new assistant U.S. attorneys with less than three years of experience who traditionally wouldn’t have been considered for such vital positions, legal experts said. Some were hired with the intent to anoint them as prosecutors — once they pass the bar exam, public disclosures show.

That figure is likely a fraction of the actual total, as a comprehensive analysis is impossible because DOJ staff identities are redacted in government personnel data . But of those ProPublica identified through bar membership records and social media, about 20 passed the bar within the last year. At least seven were in the same May graduating class as Bigley, from a range of schools.

“The fact that the DOJ is hiring, and indeed actively recruiting, right out of law school — it’s an astounding break with past practice,” said Juliet Sorensen, a Loyola University Chicago law professor and former assistant U.S. attorney. “It reflects a lowering of standards for a job that is important and requires lawyers who are meticulous, committed to doing the right thing, and bring with them experience beyond just law school.”

To understand how Trump transformed the DOJ, ProPublica examined federal court data and records, federal workforce and state bar information, and social media accounts. We also interviewed more than two dozen former assistant U.S. attorneys.

More than half of those who left the Justice Department in Trump’s first 18 months boasted nine-plus years of legal experience. Those who left had spent, on average, more than 13 years working for the government, the analysis shows. Those more experienced attorneys were the ones most likely to take on complex cases, such as money laundering, organized crime and drug trafficking, legal experts say and court dockets show.

ProPublica shared its analysis and detailed questions with the DOJ; the department did not respond. Previously, the DOJ said it “remains committed to investigating and prosecuting all types of crime.”

Under Trump’s Second Administration, Newly Hired Assistant U.S. Attorneys Have Less Experience Than Those Who Departed

The DOJ has long hired recent graduates through its Honors Program, which places graduates into rigorous training through the main office in Washington, but experts say the program was small and not meant to replace prosecutors.

Before Trump’s second term, the DOJ typically would not hire new prosecutors unless they had a minimum of three to five years of legal experience, former officials and law professors said. That standard is gone. Earlier this year, Bloomberg Law reported , the DOJ waived a policy requiring at least one year of experience.

While private law firms routinely hire promising graduates before they pass the bar exam, typically to begin their training, the DOJ’s hiring of new grads is a striking departure from its once-rigorous hiring process, said University of Michigan law professor Barbara McQuade, a former U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan.

“The people who I hired came to us as partners in law firms,” said McQuade, who was appointed by President Barack Obama. “These were superstars who had been very successful at large law firms or in state court prosecutors’ offices.”

Trump’s creation of a less experienced DOJ will have longstanding consequences, McQuade said.

“It means that some very serious crimes will go unpunished,” she said. “It takes experienced prosecutors at the federal level to bring down corporate fraud, transnational gangs and corrupt public officials.”

While experts expressed concern, some of those benefiting from the law school-to-federal prosecutor pathway have voiced excitement on LinkedIn. “I look forward to beginning my DOJ career by serving the Del Rio Division,” wrote Jacquelyn Kilcommons, who graduated from Pace University’s law school in May. “Upon receiving my bar exam results, I will transition into an Assistant United States Attorney (AUSA) position.”

As he announced his new role in the district of Washington, D.C., newly graduated assistant U.S. attorney Ellis O’Donnell wrote, “In the past few months I have had the honor to graduate from Vanderbilt University Law School and to sit for and pass the Wisconsin Bar Exam.” None of the recent law school graduates responded to requests for comment.

Shifting Personnel, Shifting Caseloads

The departure of assistant U.S. attorneys in Trump’s second administration marks the largest number of exits two years into a presidential term in at least two decades.

Beyond the personnel turnover, the administration’s priorities have shifted since Trump retook the White House, an analysis of Federal Judicial Center data shows.

As immigration cases shot up nationwide, felony fraud prosecutions fell sharply in key districts. Amid an exodus of prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia, for instance, fraud cases fell 66%. Those cases dropped 14% in the Southern District of Florida, a hotbed for white-collar crime, where many prosecutors have left in protest of Trump’s retribution campaign against people deemed political enemies. Nationally, drug prosecutions have fallen about 10% in Trump’s first 18 months and fraud cases are flat.

Meanwhile, the number of people facing immigration-related charges skyrocketed by almost 50%, clogging the courts and depleting resources at U.S. attorneys’ offices nationwide. Even in border districts where immigration proceedings can dominate the caseload, prosecutions have risen dramatically. For instance, New Mexico and the Southern District of California saw 300% and 125% increases in immigration cases, respectively, the ProPublica analysis shows. In the Western District of Texas, where Bigley and at least two other recent graduates just became prosecutors, immigration cases have surged at least 36%.

The immigration caseload, including tens of thousands of unlawful-detention cases filed in civil court, has strained the department so severely that the DOJ has drafted hundreds of attorneys from other federal agencies and the military to keep up, former officials said.

Those cases coincided with violent deportation sweeps led by masked immigration agents, who killed U.S. citizens , and the nationwide protests that sprouted up in response. Many of the cases Trump’s DOJ brought against people protesting immigration authorities’ actions fell apart, a ProPublica analysis showed . The news organization also reported how the truthfulness of Trump’s prosecutors has come under question in courts across the country. The DOJ previously said its attorneys “represent the United States with integrity.”

Amid the unrest, ProPublica has tracked nearly 100,000 habeas corpus petitions filed by immigrants arguing that their detentions were unjust. In each case, an assistant U.S. attorney must defend the government’s position, a task that had some U.S. attorneys reassigning veteran lawyers — experts in financial crimes, civil rights and human trafficking — to immigration. In Washington state, an acting U.S. attorney said he’s so overbooked with unlawful-detention petitions, his office cannot handle every case .

In South Florida, where an exodus of veteran lawyers presaged a drop in fraud and financial crime cases, one former white-collar crimes prosecutor said he and his colleagues could not decline an immigration case without permission from U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, who abruptly resigned this month. Before his resignation, Quiñones had led the “grand conspiracy” investigation targeting former officials Trump alleged were part of a “deep state” plot against him.

“Every case takes time, and you want to put in effort, and now you’re wasting your time on cases you don’t believe in or think are unjust,” said the former prosecutor, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he hopes to return to the Justice Department after Trump leaves office. “It affects morale.”

Ramping Up to Fill the Void

In recent months, the DOJ has ramped up efforts to recruit lawyers to replace the lost expertise, government data and the department’s recruiting materials show.

While Justice Department personnel data is kept secret, assistant U.S. attorneys are paid on a unique pay scale set by the attorney general, a quirk that dates to the 1950s and distinguishes them from other civil servants. By tracking the number of people compensated this way, it is possible to obtain broad data on the numbers of assistant U.S. attorneys.

As of January 2025, the department employed about 6,200 assistant U.S. attorneys, the data shows. Then Trump’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency took a hatchet to the Justice Department and other federal agencies. Led by the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, DOGE offered employees financial packages to resign from the federal government by September 2025. About 1 in 10 of all assistant U.S. attorney departures were part of that offer, the data suggests.

The ranks shrank much faster than the department anticipated, former officials said, and it was unable to hire sufficient replacements. By the end of January 2026, the DOJ lost over 1,300 assistant U.S. attorneys and replaced only about 470 of those attorneys.

More Assistant U.S. Attorneys Have Departed the Department of Justice Under Trump Than at Any Time in at Least Two Decades

For most of the past two decades, quarterly AUSA departures held fairly steady until Trump’s reelection, when they peaked at nearly 500 departures in the second quarter of 2025.

The DOJ began turning to novice attorneys to fill the empty desks.

In early 2026, a former White House official shared a post on X, the social media platform owned by Musk, that hinted at the DOJ’s growing desperation to find new hires.

“If you are a lawyer, are interested in being an AUSA, and support President Trump and anti-crime agenda, DM me,” wrote Chad Mizelle , who had recently left his DOJ role as chief of staff to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. Mizelle did not respond to a request for comment.

In March, the department hit its lowest numbers since 2014. A month later, the University of Miami hosted an event titled “Lunch & Learn: Entry Level Opportunities with The U.S. Attorney’s Office.” The invite, targeted toward third-year law students, promised a new pathway to become a criminal prosecutor in one of the country’s busiest districts.

“The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida is now recruiting 3Ls for entry-level positions beginning immediately after graduation — an exciting expansion of opportunities for Miami Law students interested in federal prosecution,” the invitation said.

To lure new hires, the DOJ is offering signing bonuses . As of August, due in part to the hiring spree focused on greener attorneys, the department lifted its ranks to about 5,600, still a 10% drop from the end of the Biden administration.

U.S. Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee and the presumed chair once Democrats take charge, told ProPublica that the shift toward inexperience is showing in courtrooms across the country.

“They’ve sacked some of the finest lawyers in America, by tradition, and replaced them with a large group of inexperienced lawyers,” said Raskin, himself an attorney.

In his home state of Maryland, fraud cases fell 31% and drug cases nearly 16%, while immigration charges nearly doubled. “Those numbers are jaw-dropping,” he said.

“Good Time to Be a … Criminal”

Jim Fang was among the veteran prosecutors who left.

Fang’s road to becoming a criminal prosecutor was winding. After working in tech for about a decade, he switched careers, and in 2009 graduated from Georgetown Law. He worked in private practice, focusing on intellectual property law, but couldn’t shake a feeling that what he really wanted was “to take down bad guys.”

In April 2020, he got his dream job and was named a federal criminal prosecutor in the District of Nevada. He moved to Las Vegas and, aided by his 11 years handling complex areas of the law, took on tough white-collar crime cases.

After the election, Trump picked Sigal Chattah , a former Republican political candidate, to run the Nevada U.S. Attorney’s Office.

Through court records and sources, ProPublica confirmed that more than 30 staff have left under Chattah’s tenure. The Nevada district is so depleted that for months it didn’t have prosecutors in its Reno office , about 450 miles away. Las Vegas prosecutors were asked to fly there for court appearances, sources said. Chattah disputed the 30 figure but acknowledged that Las Vegas-based staff flew to Reno “to ensure that our federal and local partners had competent and aggressive prosecutors.”

The office dropped cases it had been building as Chattah pushed immigration and politically motivated prosecutions . To ease the caseload, Chattah ordered her civil defense unit, charged with fighting lawsuits demanding cash from taxpayers, to pay out all cases that could be settled for $250,000 or less, multiple sources said. “We were ordered to settle those cases even if they didn’t have merit,” one former assistant U.S. attorney said. “It was just throwing money at a problem.”

Chattah called the allegations that she issued such a directive “patently false” and pushed back on her former employees’ characterizations of her tenure.

“There were attorneys that failed to meet the expectations of competent workmanship with the Department of Justice, and chose to leave or retire, some were terminated,” she wrote. “Former AUSAs who failed to handle an expected case load were replaced with aggressive prosecutors who will keep our state safe.”

In September 2025, Fang took the DOGE offer and went back into private practice as a defense attorney. He suspects the department’s loss of financial crime experts like him will result in fewer successful prosecutions.

“It’s a good time to be a white-collar criminal,” Fang said.

Now facing off against his former colleagues, he’s mostly busy representing clients who’ve filed habeas petitions. He was recently surprised to learn that one of the new hires brought into his former office had just passed the bar. “They’re taking a gamble on them,” he said.

Fang says they may well end up being fine attorneys but added, “There’s no way I could have taken that job and done it well right out of law school.”

stories.title: The Seduction of Donald Trump
stories.summary: Trump's quest to make his mark on the global stage threatens to be catastrophic. But it could be worse. The post The Seduction of Donald Trump appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and China's President Xi Jinping greet each other before the welcome banquet for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center on November 18, 2026 in Shenzhen, China (Iori Sagisawa-China Pool/Getty Images)

It was truly galling when Richard Nixon, the disgraced former U.S. president, became a respected elder statesman late in life. He published an embarrassment of a book on U.S.-Soviet relations in 1980—that nonetheless influenced incoming president Ronald Reagan. He traveled to Beijing after the Tiananmen Square massacre of 1989 in order to revive U.S.-Chinese relations by emphasizing commerce over morality. He had the ear of presidents from Ford to Clinton, which buoyed his reputation for geopolitical acuity even if what he had to say was just regurgitated realism.

Donald Trump has suffered a lifetime of disgraces—multiple bankruptcies, a gazillion lawsuits, a felony conviction, two impeachments, an election loss in 2020, and, earlier this month, a midterm repudiation. The cumulative effect of these public failures would prompt ordinary people to change their names, endure cosmetic surgery, and relocate to an obscure corner of the globe.

But shameless politicos, like Nixon and Trump, are always looking to regain the spotlight. Unlike Nixon, Trump did not try to resurrect his reputation as a post-presidential hobby. Instead he regained the Oval Office in 2024 largely to prove that he was right all along, despite all these setbacks. Over the last two years, he hasn’t made his case for redemption through arguments or by setting positive examples. Instead, he has focused on lying, bullying, and going after his enemies.

The next two years will include all of that, of course, but Trump is also likely to take a page from Nixon’s book by making his mark on international affairs. By this I don’t mean a fling with a Slovenian supermodel, though this is basically the sum total of Trump’s pre-presidential experience with foreign policy.

Trump has wanted to acquire the title of “elder statesman” ever since he returned to the Oval Office. Bagging a Nobel Peace Prize would have been an effective shortcut to this goal. To bolster his case for the prize, he has made bold claims about ending wars and heading off conflicts. By punishing bad guys—Maduro, Khamenei—he effectively styles himself as the ultimate good guy. The superpowers that he deploys—the Massive Ordnance Air Blast, the tariff, the sanction, the insult—all support his boast that he is righting historic wrongs.

In his final two years in office, Trump won’t be able to do much on the home front, thanks to a confrontational Congress. Instead, he will try to burnish—at least in his own mind—his foreign policy credentials. He will do so not through the conventional route of promoting democracy or making grand humanitarian gestures. Rather, he will stay within his comfort zone by focusing on making backroom deals with fellow strongmen.

The first stop on his two-year swan song of a world tour will be this week in Shenzhen, China.

The Troika

Once again channeling Nixon, Donald Trump wants to do something big on nuclear weapons. For Nixon, arms control negotiations were an opportunity to manage risk with the Soviet Union and, through the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, preserve the hegemonic power of the nuclear club, primarily the United States.

Trump, by contrast, doesn’t seem quite sure what he thinks about nuclear weapons.

The president has insisted that the United States has fallen behind in the nuclear race and must regain its number one position. Toward that end, the Trump administration has proposed a dramatic increase in spending on nuclear weapons to $71 billion as part of the $1.5 trillion defense budget. Over 30 years, the nuclear modernization program will cost $1.7 trillion . This is money spent, of course, on deterrence. But the president has also, from time to time, hinted at the use of nuclear weapons, most recently with his threats to annihilate Iran .

At the same time, Trump has talked about the importance of reaching nuclear arms control agreements with Russia and China. “There’s no reason for us to be building brand new nuclear weapons, we already have so many,” he said back in February 2025 , shortly after taking office. “You could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over. And here we are building new nuclear weapons, and they’re building nuclear weapons.”

That perhaps is the definition of world leader: someone who loudly laments all the money wasted on dangerous nuclear weapons even as they allocate even more funds to modernize the arsenal.

In any case, Trump is in China this week to cajole Putin and Xi into agreeing to something related to nuclear weapons. It’s going to be a heavy lift. Given the gap in size in the respective arsenals, China doesn’t believe that it has enough weapons to justify any limits. And Russia is in no mood to negotiate these days, despite the economic challenges it faces as a result of the war in Ukraine.

Actually, Trump has a lousy record when it comes to arms control. He tried to get trilateral discussions started in his first term but failed to extend the one major agreement with Russia, New START (which Biden ultimately secured). Then, in this term, Trump failed again to deal with a Russian proposal to limit deployment of nuclear weapons.

But nukes are not only thing on Trump’s mind.

A New Yalta?

Near the end of World War II, Franklin Delano Roosevelt met with Stalin and Winston Churchill at Yalta to discuss the post-war order. On the agenda was the future of Germany and Japan, the borders in and around Eastern Europe, the question of reparations, and the shape and functions of the United Nations.

Such a meeting of winners surely appeals to Trump, who wants only to sit at the big boy’s table since everything else is too low stakes for a superhero like himself. So, for instance, Trump arrived at this week’s meeting of Southeast Asian leaders so late that he could do little more than pose in the group photo. He has no interest in the United Nations, which he views solely as a once-a-year opportunity to hector the international community. He has experimented with his Board of Peace, which has barely had any effect in Gaza much less address other global problems.

Trump has put more emphasis on face-to-face meetings with Putin and Xi, though such bilateral negotiations have not yielded much either. He met Putin in Alaska last year and has conducted three sessions with Xi. The meeting with the Russian leader was all pomp and no circumstance. A few deals were concluded with Xi but nothing groundbreaking.

But a president can still dream. And Trump imagines that in Shenzhen he can put his name on a new security order in Europe, a superpower agreement on non-proliferation, perhaps even a roadmap for peace in the Middle East. All that’s required is a bit of autocrat-wrangling, which Trump prides himself on being an expert.

But the only person likely to be wrangled in Shenzhen is Trump himself. He has revealed a keen ability to be snowed by Putin, who has nimbly avoided additional sanctions and won various favors from the Trump administration in exchange for…what? The Russian leader has proven worse than uncompromising in negotiations around the war in Ukraine, most recently in Abu Dhabi where he insisted that NATO return to its pre-1997 deployments .

Instead of offering to compromise on Ukraine—on territory or security guarantees or even ceasefires—Putin is offering Trump something much dearer to the U.S. president’s heart: access to Russian fossil fuel riches.

According to The New York Times , Russia has been offering to sell off Lukoil assets—oil fields, refineries, gas stations—to a close Trump ally (Todd Boehly), two Gulf investors with ties to Jared Kushner (Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat), and an Emirati royal connected to Steve Witkoff (Sheikh Tahnoon). The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation would also get a piece of the action. Corruption, which was a top issue in the U.S. midterm elections , continues to be a guiding principle of policymaking in the Trump administration.

China has seduced Trump in a different way. It fell back on a more traditional honeypot scheme to ensnare Trump’s key computer chip ally, Jensen Huang of Nvidia. It just so happens that Nvidia is the only company that produces the chips necessary for the most powerful AI applications. And it just so happens that Huang, who was having an affair with a reputed Chinese spy, was lobbying Trump to send more of those chips to China.

Such traditional spycraft aside, China has been content to stand back and benefit from Trump’s self-inflicted wounds—the disastrous war with Iran, the tariffs against allies and adversaries, and the withdrawal from international agreements and institutions. Perhaps Trump is only accelerating U.S. decline, but China is grateful nonetheless for the revised timeline.

Putin wants to play Trump. China is happy to let Trump be Trump. They both relish the opportunity in Shenzhen to feed Trump’s delusions of grandeur. They’ll give the U.S. president a stage on which he can strut as an elder statesman. They’ll give him compliments.

But they won’t give him any real agreements.

The Next Two Years

Nixon was loathsome, to be sure, but he wasn’t stupid. Tutored by Henry Kissinger, the former president at least understood the basics of geopolitics. Also, his attempt to launder his reputation was basically harmless, at least compared to the war crimes he committed as president.

Trump, on the other hand, can do immense damage in his last two years in office. Blocked by Congress from doing more DOGE-like damage to the U.S. government, he will turn his attention to furthering his campaign to destroy international institutions. The war the administration has launched against the International Criminal Court will serve as a model.

The seduction of Trump by Putin and Xi—along with lesser autocrats like Modi, Erdogan, and Milei—could have even more damaging consequences. Putin will wield Trump like a machete to cut the strings that hold together NATO and the European Union. China will use Trump’s anti-internationalism to remake global affairs in its own image—mercantile, extractivist, autocratic. Trump, seduced, will think that he is at the helm, an elder statesman coming into his own, putting his mark on the world much as he is making his mark on Washington, DC.

With Trump, this might be the best-case scenario. The alternative—increased conflict with Russia or China or both—would be even more catastrophic. Yes, it’s a horrifying prospect, but let Trump believe that he is remaking the world.

It’s better than his unmaking of it.

stories.title: What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry
stories.summary: The post What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry appeared first on NOEMA .

stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature. Mei’s case was hailed by Chinese media as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain. stories.title: Venezuela’s Base Deal Has No Voters
stories.summary: Venezuelans deserve democracy before, not after, a military deal with the United States. The post Venezuela’s Base Deal Has No Voters appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright speaks with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez during a press conference regarding the oil agreement reached by the US government and Venezuela on September 2, 2026 in Caracas, Venezuela. (Jesus Vargas/Getty Images)

In his first week as Venezuela’s foreign minister, Oliver Blanco sat down with Marco Rubio at the State Department on November 2. The official readout spoke of electoral reforms, political prisoners and the president’s three-phase plan : stabilization first, then economic recovery and reconciliation, and only then a democratic transition. It said nothing about soldiers.

A day later, The New York Times reported that the State Department, under Rubio, is negotiating a status of forces agreement with Caracas that would lay the foundation for a long-term American military presence. Troop numbers and locations would be settled in later agreements.

Washington will sell this as paperwork. The State Department says it has negotiated such pacts with more than 100 countries, which give American forces a predictable legal footing for ship visits, training, and exercises. Seen from outside Washington, Venezuela is not merely the latest entry on that list. It is a country whose president was seized by American troops on January 3 , whose interim leader holds no electoral mandate, and whose oil now carries a Pentagon stake.

A status of forces agreement signed under those conditions does not regulate a relationship between two sovereign governments. It writes a protectorate into law before the protected get a vote.

The soldiers, in fact, are arriving ahead of the lawyers. On October 30, Venezuelan drones and helicopters struck a Colombian National Liberation Army (ELN) camp in Apure state near the border with Colombia, and four U.S. officials told The Times that Washington supplied intelligence and drone support. The border rights group FundaRedes counted 23 victim s . Back in June, a Southern Command airstrike killed Héctor Rusthenford Guerrero Flores, a founder of Tren de Aragua, with CIA intelligence and Venezuelan forces taking part. After the June earthquakes, about 2,000 American troops moved into and around the country before pulling out again. The reopened U.S. embassy in Caracas already has a military attaché.

The readout leaves out an important motive for a future military base: the oil fields. In September, the administration announced a deal giving Washington a stake in about one-fifth of Venezuela’s oil resources. Caracas handed North American Blue Energy Partners, the vehicle of oilman Alejandro Betancourt, 100-year rights over 17 oilfields holding 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. The Pentagon owns 35 percent of that company, and Washington is guaranteed the right to buy a fifth of its output at cost.

Nobody leaves a century-long concession, part-owned by the Defense Department, without a guard. Donald Trump , speaking in Washington the same Monday Blanco visited, did not bother with euphemism. He referred to “our conquest of Venezuela.” Oil contracts are written for decades. So, it seems, are the garrisons that guard them.

Latin America has lived through this imbroglio before. In 1901, Cuba had to accept the Platt Amendment before American forces would leave, and the State Department’s historians list among its conditions the sale or lease of land for naval stations. The Guantánamo lease followed in February 1903. Washington repealed the amendment in 1934 and kept the lease, and the naval base still operates. The political tutelage was renegotiated. The military footprint signed during the tutelage outlived everyone who signed it.

The interim authority across the table from Rubio is in no position to bargain hard, and it has no mandate to bargain at all. Delcy Rodríguez has given no election date. Trump says Venezuela is not ready for elections. María Corina Machado, back after ten months in exile, wants a presidential vote by July. On Monday, teachers, nurses and university unions held a 12-hour national stoppage , demanding a $960 year-end payment that the government had left unanswered . The minimum monthly income stands at $240 . A government that cannot settle with its teachers is settling the legal status of foreign soldiers. Venezuelans can read that order of priorities. So can every capital in the hemisphere.

The counterargument deserves a fair hearing. Status of forces agreements are mundane instruments, and most of them govern exercises rather than occupations. The ELN and Tren de Aragua are real, and a Venezuelan army that sheltered guerrillas for years is now bombing them. The State Department insists that no base talks are under way.

But that is exactly the design of the deal. The framework comes first, and everything that matters (numbers, locations, duration) would be part of follow-on arrangements that neither an elected Venezuelan legislature nor the U.S. Senate will ever vote on.

The Democratic majorities that won both chambers on November 3 have three ways to keep this interim arrangement from hardening.

First, demand the text. State Department officials briefed some congressional aides on the talks in late October. A briefing for aides is not oversight.

Second, insist on the treaty form. Basing and status arrangements are usually concluded as executive agreements, not treaties. Venezuela is the case for the exception. An open-ended military presence in a country the United States attacked 10 months ago is the kind of commitment the Constitution leaves to two-thirds of the Senate.

Third, use the purse. A rider barring funds for any permanent presence in Venezuela until an elected government ratifies the arrangement would cost Washington nothing it needs this year. It would cost the oil concession its armed guarantee, and for obvious reasons the White House will fight it.

The timing gives the game away. If Rubio signs the agreement before the new Congress convenes in January, an outgoing majority and an unelected partner will have settled the matter between them, and Venezuelans will inherit the deal the way Cubans inherited Guantánamo. If the deal waits for a Senate vote and an elected government in Caracas, it may still go through. At least it will have voters behind it.
