stories.title: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
stories.summary: Andy Burnham wants "steps" towards a closer EU alignment. But the bloc has changed considerably since the UK left it
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left

Published 18 November 2026

"Opening the door to uncontrolled immigration," is how Reform UK described it. "Dragging us into the European Union via the back door," was the charge levelled by the Conservatives.

You could be forgiven for expecting drastic change come Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels judging by some of the criticism levelled by opponents of the Labour government.

Instead, what's on the table is a limited youth work and mobility scheme (the source of Reform's ire), agreement on cross-channel carbon emissions pricing and a deal to ease food trade.

There's also talk of reducing tuition fees for EU students at British universities (something EU member states, like Germany, really want) in exchange for the UK being admitted to an EU manufacturing scheme (which is important to the Burnham government).

Even in these limited areas, I'm told, not all details will be ironed out by the time of Friday's meeting.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted last week this is all a "step" towards a closer working relationship with Europe.

It's certainly not a leap, and definitely not a matter of rejoining the bloc at this stage.

Other "steps" under immediate discussion are the UK rejoining the EU's electricity market, and the UK trying again to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme.

"Small steps… to make both sides stronger," is how the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas describes this process. She also warns: "We have in Europe a lot of trauma from Britain leaving [the EU], so things will not be easy."

At this week's summit, the UK and EU are expected to discuss a limited youth mobility scheme, cross-channel carbon emissions pricing, and a deal to ease food trade

Bigger, potentially more politically explosive EU-UK questions look likely to follow after Friday's summit. It's thought Burnham may propose rejoining the EU's customs union and/or the single market. There are suggestions he could eventually table a new referendum on rejoining the EU. None of this before the next general election, though.

On this side of the Channel, the debate is very much focused on what Britain might want. Burnham's plan is bold, belated or completely barmy - depending on your political perspective. But there's been little discussion about the EU point of view, and less still on how the EU has changed since Britain left it.

Just how different is the EU in 2026 from the bloc Britain turned its back on a decade ago? And with the UK still mired in arguments over its relationship with Europe, does the EU even want GB back in the fold or would Brussels now rather avoid more drama?

A series of shocks

Since 2016, a series of international shocks have fundamentally changed the EU.

The Covid crisis collapsed international supply chains. Europe became aware just how dependent it was on China for medical supplies, for example. Then, Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine showed the EU how utterly reliant many members were on energy supplies from Moscow. Big EU beasts like Germany and Italy were particularly affected.

The Ukraine war, the continent's biggest active conflict since World War Two, has persuaded the EU that Europe's domestic defence industry and industrial policy needs a boost and far better coordination.

Donald Trump's two stints as US president convinced the EU that it can never again fully rely on the US to be Europe's best friend abroad, either in trade or security terms. And China's attempt to 'dump' cheap cars and steel in Europe, hurting the Continent's businesses, has made the EU more protectionist-minded.

Brussels's main takeaways: Europe should become more self-reliant. And where imports are needed - with fossil fuels, for example - it must diversify which countries it buys from.

The French used to be a lone voice amongst big EU countries, pushing for more protectionism. Other member states prioritised finding the lowest possible prices, as was once the case with Russian gas, for example. Now there's a growing acceptance that economic efficiency must at times be sacrificed to achieve security of supply.

Some think the UK won't want to align itself with an increasingly protectionist, borrow-happy bloc. While an EU member, the free-trade-minded UK was credited with pushing Brussels to be more "British" and make its single market more competitive.

Britain's 2016 EU referendum prompted years of political drama

Others point out that Britain has also changed since 2016.

"The British are less 'British' than they once were," Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform, told me. When the EU introduced steel tariffs to protect itself against Chinese dumping, the UK followed suit with its own, similar tariffs. Now, the EU is placing high tariffs on Chinese imports of electric vehicles - and once again the UK is considering a similar move. "Everyone is a bit more French now," says Grant.

Another big EU change, according to Georgina Wright, a senior adviser at the German Marshall Fund, is that EU citizens have become more comfortable with the idea of centralised European power: a pooling of sovereignty in times of emergency.

The Covid crisis prompted the EU to embrace 'common borrowing', where Brussels raises debt on behalf of member states, who then share the benefits and the risks. It was a historic move, particularly for Germany which was once allergic to the idea. Now there's discussion about a new round of common borrowing focused on defence, in answer to Russian aggression and a US proposing to withdraw defence capabilities from Europe.

Some in the EU tell me that none of this would be possible had the more sovereign-minded UK remained a member state.

A changing EU

But there are political winds of change blowing through the bloc.

Nationalist, more Eurosceptic parties are polling strongly in big EU members states ahead of upcoming elections. The EU that Burnham wants Britain to align with might look very different by the end of next year.

In France, one of the EU's two most influential countries, the hard-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading opinion polls ahead of the spring presidential election. Nation-first parties in Italy, Spain and Poland, as in France, say they want to transform the bloc from the inside.

Britain's centre-left government - as well as some UK voters - might be put off by an EU with Le Pen as a dominant force.

Conversely, there's an argument that an EU led by Eurosceptics might actually become more appealing to Britain. While those parties have their differences, they generally want to take powers back from Brussels, making the EU a looser club of stronger nation states - less of a political project, and more of a transactional club of common economic interests.

One change we can pretty much bet on is this: if Le Pen becomes French president, Brussels will become embroiled in internal existential tussles over the EU's future. These fault lines will pit the left against the right; pro-Europeans against Eurosceptics; Ukraine backers against those (like Le Pen) who want to stop financial aid; fans of a bigger EU budget against parties wanting to slash national contributions.

With all that going on, negotiations with the UK would very likely slip further down the priority list. British diplomats might find their calls unanswered.

If Burnham really wants to get closer to the EU, the time to act is now, says Wright. She identifies a window of opportunity before France's election for the UK to get "creative" in its re-set proposals.

Marine Le Pen leads the polls in France for next year's presidential election

Brussels is certainly under pressure to be more flexible in its relations with trusted allies outside the bloc, because of the threatening geopolitical climate. The EU embrace of Canada is a clear example.

"The prime minister should get out and about on the continent more, be more visible and talk more positively about what can be done together," says Wright.

Wright insists people in the UK are open to the idea. She quotes a survey by the National Centre for Social Research, published this month, which suggests 42% of Britons prioritise closer links with Europe over the US, while only 9% of Britons prioritise links with the US.

What Brussels wants

Then there's the question of how much Brussels actually wants Britain back in the European bloc.

Some in the UK believe they could take advantage of current geopolitical uncertainty. With the Russian threat looming, they think Brussels wants to have the UK close because of the UK's military and nuclear capabilities. In exchange, the UK could push for an ambitious deal with the EU, says Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey.

But Dr Ilke Toygür, a politics professor at Madrid's IE University, points out that European countries already work closely with the UK in defence, through Nato and the British and French-led support for Ukraine - so UK military leverage may not matter so much in EU terms.

Having the UK back in the European Union would certainly give the bloc more economic heft. In fact, some in the UK argue Britain is far better outside the bloc. Member states' economies are struggling, they say: look at stagnant Germany and Italy, and spluttering France. The UK, on the other hand, has grown at its fastest rate in two years thanks to AI investment. The UK enjoys freedom to regulate the AI industry outside the EU that it wouldn't have as an EU member state.

But EU diplomats I speak to believe the UK needs Brussels more than the other way round.

Germany and some European countries are investing in defence - and Britain now wants to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme

"The UK alone is a middling power in a field of giants," an EU diplomat from a big European country told me. He asked to remain anonymous in order to speak freely. "With China on the one side and the US on the other, the UK will be trampled underfoot if it stands alone. It must know that."

If the UK were ever to rejoin the EU, he says, it wouldn't necessarily have to join the euro currency or the open-border Schengen scheme.

But Michel Barnier, the former EU lead Brexit negotiator, tells me that as long as Britain remains outside the bloc it can't just cherry-pick all the benefits . It's the same argument the UK faced during cross-channel talks 10 years ago. The EU views the single market as the jewel in the bloc's crown, says Barnier, and Brussels does not want to devalue it by making major exceptions for the UK that other non-EU countries would then demand too. But he adds that the UK remains a much-appreciated ally and trading partner.

It would help Burnham, says the academic Toygür, if the UK had a more positive story to tell. She says Brussels is used to hearing Britain saying "we want to get closer to the EU because it's better for UK economic interests". Instead they should emphasise benefits to the EU, she says.

"We face a competition of great powers (China, US, Russia) and we are stronger together.

"The UK needs to commit resources: innovation and financial capacities to a continental-level project. It doesn't have to call that project 'the EU' but this is the only story moving forward."

What you hear from EU diplomats is that member states are more than OK with the existing post-Brexit trade deal. There is not a huge appetite to unravel it and start again.

The "little steps" of change, beneficial to both sides, like easing exports and imports, are what the EU is comfortable with right now.

Still, economist Heather Grabbe, from the Brussels-based economic think-tank Bruegel, predicts an "inevitable drift together" between the two sides.

British universities have historically been popular with Europeans - and now Brussels wants the UK to lower tuition fees for EU students

"We face the same challenges: aging populations, wildfires and storms, the impact of climate change, with our continent warming at twice the global rate. Russia is attacking us all with its hybrid warfare, we have the same outlook in world affairs: we're not pro-Trump, we're not pro-Putin. Working together makes sense," she says.

EU countries express a lot of warmth when asked about the UK inching closer. But behind closed doors, there is clear reticence. "Commitment" is a word you hear over and again; they're not sure that Britain really means it. They hear the Conservative Party deputy leader, Alex Burghart, for example, who vowed that, if elected, his party would "rip up" Labour's upcoming UK-EU agreements.

"The UK first needs a national conversation. And a binding decision. They need to know what they want and stick to it," say EU figures I speak to.

This is exactly what the EU insisted on 10 years ago, after the UK voted for Brexit without a clear political plan for what future relations with the bloc should look like.

As a journalist who's covered the UK's divorce from the EU right from the outset, I'm getting a rather strong sense of déjà vu.

stories.summary: The UK could miss legally binding climate targets if EV targets are cut, an adviser warns
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Current rules say all new cars must be zero emission by 2035

Published 18 November 2026

The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.

In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".

The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.

The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.

Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.

Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".

Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.

In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.

But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars

SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.

"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.

Carbon budget

The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.

The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.

CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise.

Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money".

He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".

A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

stories.title: Burnham to set out options next month for long-term EU relationship
stories.summary: The prime minister says he will set out options for the future "alongside" his 10-year economic plan.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026

Andy Burnham has said he plans to set out his proposed options to reshape the UK's future relationship with the EU next month.

Downing Street had been facing pressure to specify when the prime minister would take this step, after he previously said he would do so "around" a summit taking place in Brussels this week.

Burnham will travel to the meeting with the EU this Friday, where both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

However, it is understood he will not indicate any preference at this stage which of the long-term options he could back in future.

Former Prime Minister Boris Johnson said Burnham would be wasting his premiership by reopening arguments about Brexit.

Speaking to Sky News, Burnham said: "I'm in a negotiation about improving the Brexit deal - that's what I'm doing this week. We'll see how it goes.

"And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU."

He added this would be set out "alongside" the 10-year plan for the economy that he has promised to unveil before Parliament breaks for Christmas.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Negotiations for the deals to be unveiled on Friday began under Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, but Burnham has indicated he believes the UK's Brexit deal needs to be revised further.

Making his first major foreign policy speech on Monday night, Burnham told his audience: "After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship.

"This will take time, and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next Parliament."

In September, Burnham told the Labour Party conference he would "take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with our European partners".

Asked on Tuesday whether Burnham was now "hitting the brakes" and pushing any announcement of options back further into the future, a No 10 spokesman said earlier: "I don't accept that characterisation."

And speaking to Sky News, Burnham rejected the idea he was stepping back, arguing he was "doing exactly what I said".

"I will set out next month what the next phase looks like, and that is exactly what I said at my conference speech."

Former Foreign Secretary David Lammy has said Labour should go into the next election promising to rejoin the EU.

Writing in The Times on Tuesday, , external he said the prime minister's conference speech in Liverpool "didn't only ignite a debate around joining the EU - it blew the door wide open".

"Burnham is right to break glass on the European question because membership is the greatest growth accelerator the government has available."

'Madness'

He also dismissed Johnson's warning against reopening arguments about Brexit.

Johnson had told the Daily Telegraph , external : "It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority.

"He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won't win – because the reality is that people are not fools."

Responding to his comments, Burnham said: "I just don't think he's an authority on these matters.

"I'm afraid I'm not going to listen to Boris Johnson on this particular matter. He burned bridges and created a lot of bad feeling, and consequently, Britain suffered as a result of that."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage MP said Burnham was "turning his back" on his constituents in Makerfield, where two-thirds of residents voted for Brexit in the 2016 referendum.

"We haven't taken the full advantage of Brexit and the idea of tying us back to single market rules overseen by the [European Court of Justice] is nothing less than a democratic outrage," he added.

stories.title: Voters Reject ALPRs and Surveillance Tech at the Ballot Box
stories.summary: Do automated license plate readers (ALPRs) have any place in our communities? That question has been a hot topic in city council meetings , community conversations , and news coverage around the country for months. This past election day, a couple of U.S communities took it further: to the ballot. And overwhelmingly, voters decided that, no, these devices should not be deployed on our streets. We agree! In Maine, the coastal community of York voted to remove the town’s existing ALPR cameras and require that any future proposed installations receive voter approval before proceeding. The local initiative ended up on the ballot after constituents gathered enough signatures on a citizens’ petition for a local ordinance. On Election Day, nearly three-quarters of York voters supported the ban. Thousands of miles away, voters in League City, Texas also voted against allowing the local police department to continue use of ALPR cameras. That vote was formally approved on November 17, which began a 72-hour window to remove the cameras. Since the election, the cameras have been “bagged” or covered to prevent the collection of data. At least one city also decided to expand protections afforded to their residents when it comes to the use of surveillance technology. In Pflugerville, Texas, Proposition B passed , now requiring that the City Charter be amended to include “protections governing the collection, use, retention, and oversight of data, facial recognition, and surveillance technologies.” It also requires “a responsible artificial intelligence framework.” While every municipality has different rules for how to get a local ordinance placed on the ballot, banning use and securing the removal of surveillance tools locally is a powerful way of protecting your community against devices and data collection that goes far beyond your town lines. Surveillance is a choice, not a mandate, and our communities have the power to refuse it. EFF has supported local communities around the country over the last few years in advocating against the procurement of surveillance technologies in their cities, counties, and states. These victories at the ballot box and in city councils show that when mass surveillance is presented as a policy choice, not a technical necessity, communities can and do reject it. Do you know what surveillance tools are being used by your local police…

stories.title: The Justice Department Wants To Give Patent Trolls More Power
stories.summary: Software patents are mostly vague, hard to define, and widely abused. Most tech patent lawsuits aren’t filed by companies that make real products. They’re filed by patent trolls, companies that acquire patents to extract payments through litigation and legal threats. A patent on one feature of a smartphone shouldn’t give the patent owner the power to threaten the existence of the entire product line. But that is exactly the leverage patent trolls want—and the current administration is helping them to get it. In two recent patent cases, Radian Memory Systems v. Samsung and Collision Communications v. Samsung, the Justice Department and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office have asked courts to make it easier for patent owners to get injunctions. These are judicial orders that can force companies to stop selling products or remove features from them, rather than simply pay monetary damages. The threat of an injunction can pressure a company to pay far more than what a patent is actually worth. In 2006, NTP Inc., a patent holding company with no products of its own, was able to pressure BlackBerry manufacturer Research in Motion Ltd. to pay a $612 million settlement when it was on the verge of an injunction. Protection Against Patent Trolls In May 2006, the Supreme Court rejected the practice of granting permanent injunctions almost automatically after a finding of patent infringement. In eBay v. MercExchange , the high court held that patent owners must satisfy the same tough requirements that plaintiffs in non-patent cases must meet to get a permanent injunction. After eBay, patent owners had to show “irreparable harm,” that they can’t be adequately compensated by money, that the “balance of hardships” favors the plaintiff, and, critically, that an injunction would not harm the “public interest.” At EFF, we celebrated eBay v. MercExchange as a major win for internet users. More than twenty years ago, we saw that software patents were going to be a disaster—not just for small companies (which they are), but for freedom of expression online. As EFF explained in its brief : The United States Patent and Trademark Office has issued patents on methods for downloading video programs , publishing web pages , sending email messages, making internet telephone calls , and even online fundraising methods. stories.title: The Paramount-Warner Brothers Deal Could Usher in Another Age of Lost Media
stories.summary: There are all sorts of reasons to be against the merger of Paramount and Warner Brothers-Discovery. There's the obvious problem of increasing concentration in the already pretty-concentrated film and TV industry. People have problems with Paramount's owner Skydance interfering with its news coverage and late night comedy . But one of the biggest is the way we are losing choice and access to information and culture. In the context of the digital world, there are two major problems with these mega mergers. One, as we've said in the past, is that it further degrades the already awful state of mainstream streaming services. In short, by increasing the amount of legacy content under their control, major studios don't have to invest in either new content or well-engineered services to get users. Plus, they can pool the data they have on users together in an increasing assault on consumer privacy. A monthly subscription and more information about your habits and interests? Win-win for them. Another problem is the disappearing of content. In the digital era, there should be no more lost media. Making and storing copies of media is easier and cheaper than it ever has been. The idea of the persistence of content online has become the adage "the internet never forgets." However, since more and more media is locked behind subscription services under the control of fewer and fewer companies—and as physical copies, or even just digital copies that are actually owned by consumers also vanish—access to our common culture is at risk. Incentives to take information and media offline should raise huge red flags. Unfortunately, they are multiplying. First, there's the impulse of merged companies to offset the cost of their merger by shelving projects and claiming them as tax write-offs. We saw this the last time Warner Brothers was taken over, with projects being ended in order to take advantage of a specific kind of tax benefit. It has little to do with the quality or even how much or how complete a project is—money is the driving factor and we as a culture are all poorer for it. And we all know it. stories.title: European Commission Plan to Give Frontex Trusted Flagger Status Is A Threat to Free Speech
stories.summary: EFF and 27 other human rights organizations called on the European Commission today to retract a dangerous proposal granting its border agency Frontex power to request that national authorities issue takedown orders for social media content and giving Frontext “trusted flagger” status under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU regulation governing online platforms and content moderation in the region. The extraordinarily improper proposal not only disregards the provisions of the DSA but also places a mechanism of enforcement overreach in the hands of a law enforcement agency that has failed to safeguard people against serious human rights violations at EU borders. Under the proposal , Frontex has the power to “monitor publicly accessible social media content, detect developments relevant to external border management, and support action against illegal online content linked to border-security risks.” Granting Frontex trusted flagger privileges on top of its existing mandate risks creating a powerful tool for over-enforcement, stifling the free expression of migrants, asylum seekers, and other marginalized groups. We warned the Commission of these risks in a letter . The DSA is supposed to make online platforms more accountable and protect users’ fundamental rights, not give the EU power to sic its border police on people for exercising their right to free expression. EFF and other rights organizations have for years sounded alarms about potential abuse under the DSA’s trusted flagger provision, which gives “Digital Services Coordinators” the ability to award entities—including law enforcement agencies—a privileged channel to alert online platforms about illegal content. We’ve taken the firm position that law enforcement cannot be trusted to properly flag illegal content. In July, we told the Commission that giving law enforcement trusted flagger status could undermine fundamental rights and said that police agencies like Frontex should not be made trusted flaggers. stories.title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
stories.summary: The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches. Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols , these incidents likely would not have occurred. While the White House and some leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate new protocols are largely unnecessary. Following existing best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems. Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code. Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so.
